Hear my thoughts? No, I don't think so. That's... that's not how the brain works, scientifically speaking. It's all electrical impulses and synapses, contained in the skull.

Well, yes, like I just said, it's definitely been more than a month. The certainty that people on the project are tracking my revisions and planting those errors has been there for about the last two months. 

I know because I mark everything down on my desk calendar. It's one of those big paper blotter calendars with the faux-leather corners. You don't see those much anymore, really, because everyone relies on digital calendars now. But the problem with digital calendars is the server synchronization. If there's a latency issue between the local client and the exchange server, you can get conflicting data. The timestamp protocols—like NTP, Network Time Protocol—are supposed to prevent that by keeping all the system clocks synced to within milliseconds of Coordinated Universal Time. They use these atomic clocks, usually cesium or rubidium, which measure the exact electromagnetic radiation of electron transitions. It's incredibly precise. I read a paper recently explaining that the primary atomic clock in Colorado is so accurate it won't lose a single second in a hundred million years. 

A hundred million years... it really makes you wonder what the earth's topography will even look like then. Because tectonic plate drift averages about one and a half centimeters a year, depending on the fault line, so over a hundred million years, the continents will be completely unrecognizable. The Pacific Ocean might just close up entirely, pushing California right up against Japan. The subduction zones would create massive volcanic activity... 

But, uh, yes. More than a month. Two months.

Less sleep? No, no, I don't think so. I usually get my seven or eight hours. I've never really had a time where I didn't need to sleep and still felt energized. Depressed? No, I don't think so. I wouldn't say I feel sad or down most of the day. I'm mostly just preoccupied with the data inconsistencies at work. My mood itself is actually fairly stable.

Voices? No, no, I haven't heard any voices. The house is usually quite silent when I'm alone. Well, except for the ambient noise, of course. True silence is actually quite rare. The threshold of human hearing is generally considered to be zero decibels, but that's just a reference point for a sound wave with a pressure of 20 micropascals. 

I was reading about anechoic chambers recently. They're these highly specialized rooms designed to completely absorb reflections of either sound or electromagnetic waves. They line the walls, floor, and ceiling with these deep, wedge-shaped fiberglass acoustic absorbers. The geometry of the wedges is critical because it forces the sound waves to bounce back and forth deep within the structure of the foam, dissipating the acoustic energy as trace amounts of heat. Microsoft actually built the quietest place on Earth at their headquarters in Washington. The background noise level there is negative 20.6 decibels. New drugs? No, no new medications or anything like that. I just take my regular blood pressure pill, the same one I've been on for years. 

Speaking of pharmaceuticals, the pharmacokinetic modeling involved in drug development is just astounding these days. They use these massive compartmental models to simulate how a compound distributes through the body's tissues over time. The rate of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion—the ADME profile—is all governed by differential equations. It's really just a specialized application of mass transfer kinetics. The liver, for instance, acts as this incredible biochemical reactor. The cytochrome P450 enzymes in the hepatic cells are responsible for metabolizing the vast majority of xenobiotics. They catalyze the oxidation of organic substances. The molecular docking simulations they run now to predict how a new drug molecule will bind to those enzyme active sites require immense computational power. They use Monte Carlo algorithms to sample all the possible conformational states of the protein-ligand complex. It's basically a highly sophisticated optimization problem, trying to find the lowest free energy state of the system. 

It reminds me of the protein folding problem, actually. For decades, it was considered computationally intractable to predict a protein's three-dimensional structure just from its amino acid sequence. The number of possible conformations is astronomically large—Levinthal's paradox, they call it. If a protein tried every possible fold sequentially, it would take longer than the age of the universe to find the right one. But in reality, they fold in milliseconds. Now, with deep learning models like AlphaFold, they've practically solved it using attention-based neural networks...

But, uh, no. I haven't started any new medications. Just the usual ones.

Emotionally flat? I guess... I guess you could say that. It's like I was just saying about the telescope and the hiking and the astronomy nights. I used to really get a kick out of those things, especially mentoring the younger analysts at the office. Seeing them grasp a complex concept for the first time... it used to feel good. This flatness problem was actually one of the main catalysts for the theory of cosmic inflation. But, uh, yes. Emotionally, I suppose I do feel quite flat. I just don't experience that pleasure anymore.

This flatness problem was actually one of the main catalysts for the theory of cosmic inflation. If the early universe underwent an exponential expansion in a fraction of a second, it would have stretched out any initial curvature, making the universe appear flat to us today, much like how the Earth appears flat from our localized perspective on the surface. Well, let's see... six months? No, it's been quite a bit longer than that. This whole... decline, I suppose you could call it, really started after I was put in charge of the larger environmental modeling contract. That was about two years and two months ago. 

Environmental modeling is such a complex undertaking. You're dealing with coupled non-linear partial differential equations to simulate fluid dynamics in the atmosphere and oceans. The Navier-Stokes equations, for instance, are notoriously difficult to solve. They describe the motion of viscous fluid substances, and the existence and smoothness of solutions to these equations in three dimensions is actually one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems in mathematics. If you can prove it, the Clay Mathematics Institute will give you a million dollars.

It's essentially trying to predict the unpredictable. Lorenz was a meteorologist, you know, and he discovered strange attractors while running weather simulations on a Royal McBee LGP-30 computer in the 1960s. The Lorenz attractor looks like a butterfly, ironically enough. It's a fractal structure, meaning it has a non-integer dimension. Fractals are everywhere in nature—coastlines, snowflakes, the branching of blood vessels... 

But, um, yes. The contract. That was about two years and two months ago, and that's when this all started.

Voices? No... no, I haven't experienced anything like that. Just the normal ambient sounds, you know. 

Sound is an interesting phenomenon, though, when you really break it down. It's purely mechanical—longitudinal waves of pressure propagating through a medium like air or water. Unlike electromagnetic radiation, which can travel through the vacuum of space, sound absolutely requires matter to vibrate. The speed of sound in dry air at standard atmospheric pressure is roughly 343 meters per second, but that changes depending on the temperature and the density of the medium. In water, it's over four times faster. 

That's the fundamental principle behind sonar, actually—Sound Navigation and Ranging. Submarines use it to navigate and detect targets in the deep ocean. They send out an acoustic pulse, a 'ping', and measure the time it takes for the echo to return. If the target is moving, the frequency of the return echo will be altered due to the Doppler effect. Christian Doppler described that mathematically in 1842. It's the same reason an ambulance siren noticeably drops in pitch as it drives past you on the street. The sound waves get compressed as the vehicle approaches and stretched out as it recedes. We actually use the exact same principle in astrophysics, but with light waves instead of sound, to measure the redshift of distant galaxies. Edwin Hubble used the relativistic Doppler effect to prove the universe is expanding, which completely upended Einstein's cosmological constant...

Well, let me think about the timeline there. The certainty that people on the project are tracking my revisions and planting errors... that specific realization has been there for about the last two months. But before that? Yes, the withdrawal and the... the flatness, that was already happening. 

It's fascinating how timelines intersect, isn't it? Like the intersection of two non-parallel lines in a Euclidean plane. They have exactly one point in common. But if you consider lines in three-dimensional space, they can be skew lines—lines that are neither parallel nor intersecting. They exist in different planes entirely. The shortest distance between two skew lines can be calculated using the cross product of their directional vectors. 

Vectors are incredibly useful in physics. A vector has both magnitude and direction, unlike a scalar, which only has magnitude. Temperature is a scalar, but velocity is a vector. If you want to calculate the work done by a force, you take the dot product of the force vector and the displacement vector. The dot product yields a scalar, which is why work is measured in Joules, a scalar quantity. James Prescott Joule, the English brewer and physicist, established the mechanical equivalent of heat in the 1840s. He used a falling weight to spin a paddle wheel in an insulated barrel of water, proving that mechanical work could be converted directly into thermal energy. It was a crucial step in formulating the First Law of Thermodynamics, the conservation of energy...

But, yes. The flatness was definitely there before I realized what they were doing with the errors. The errors started about two months ago.

You see it everywhere, from global weather patterns to the aerodynamic wake of a commercial airliner. \n\nA Boeing 777, for instance, creates massive wingtip vortices. It's a byproduct of lift, where the high-pressure air beneath the wing seeks the low-pressure area above it, creating these violent horizontal tornadoes that can linger in the air for miles. That's exactly why air traffic controllers have to enforce strict wake turbulence separation minima between heavy aircraft and smaller planes. If a little Cessna flies into a 777's wake, the induced roll can completely overwhelm the aircraft's control authority. The physics of it are just unforgiving...\n\nBut, uh, no. I haven't been feeling depressed.\n\nDoctor: Have you been hearing voices when no one else is around?\n\nPatient: Voices? No, no, I haven't heard any voices. The house is usually quite silent when I'm alone. Well, except for the ambient noise, of course. True silence is actually quite rare. The threshold of human hearing is generally considered to be zero decibels, but that's just a reference point for a sound wave with a pressure of 20 micropascals. \n\nI was reading about anechoic chambers recently. They're these highly specialized rooms designed to completely absorb reflections of either sound or electromagnetic waves. They line the walls, floor, and ceiling with these deep, wedge-shaped fiberglass acoustic absorbers. The geometry of the wedges is critical because it forces the sound waves to bounce back and forth deep within the structure of the foam, dissipating the acoustic energy as trace amounts of heat. Microsoft actually built the quietest place on Earth at their headquarters in Washington. The background noise level there is negative 20.6 decibels. It's so quiet that you can hear your own heartbeat, the blood rushing through your veins, and even the grinding of your bones when you move. It's fascinating, but people who go in there often start experiencing sensory deprivation hallucinations within just a few minutes. The brain is essentially a pattern-recognition engine, and when you deprive it of external stimuli, it just starts generating its own internal signals to compensate. It's the same mechanism behind phantom limb pain in amputees. The somatosensory cortex is still looking for input from the missing limb, and when it doesn't get any, it creates the sensation of pain...\n\nBut, um, no. To answer your question, I haven't been hearing any voices.\n\nDoctor: Have you started using any new drugs or medications in the past few months?\n\nPatient: New drugs? No, no new medications or anything like that. I just take my regular blood pressure pill, the same one I've been on for years. \n\nSpeaking of pharmaceuticals, the pharmacokinetic modeling involved in drug development is just astounding these days. They use these massive compartmental models to simulate how a compound distributes through the body's tissues over time. The rate of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion—the ADME profile—is all governed by differential equations. It's really just a specialized application of mass transfer kinetics. The liver, for instance, acts as this incredible biochemical reactor. The cytochrome P450 enzymes in the hepatic cells are responsible for metabolizing the vast majority of xenobiotics. They catalyze the oxidation of organic substances. The molecular docking simulations they run now to predict how a new drug molecule will bind to those enzyme active sites require immense computational power. They use Monte Carlo algorithms to sample all the possible conformational states of the protein-ligand complex. It's basically a highly sophisticated optimization problem, trying to find the lowest free energy state of the system. \n\nIt reminds me of the protein folding problem, actually. For decades, it was considered computationally intractable to predict a protein's three-dimensional structure just from its amino acid sequence. The number of possible conformations is astronomically large—Levinthal's paradox, they call it. If a protein tried every possible fold sequentially, it would take longer than the age of the universe to find the right one. But in reality, they fold in milliseconds. Now, with deep learning models like AlphaFold, they've practically solved it using attention-based neural networks...\n\nBut, uh, no. I haven't started any new medications. Just the usual ones.\n\nDoctor: Have you found yourself feeling much less motivated than usual to do things?\n\nPatient: Motivated? Well, I suppose I have been. It's a Schmidt-Cassegrain design. Beautiful piece of engineering, really. It uses a catadioptric optical system, which combines a primary spherical mirror with a secondary convex mirror and a refractive corrector plate to eliminate spherical aberration. Spherical aberration is a fascinating optical flaw. It happens when incoming parallel light rays striking the outer edges of a spherical mirror focus at a slightly different point along the optical axis than the rays striking the center. It completely ruins the image resolution, creating this soft, blurred halo effect. \n\nThat's exactly what happened with the Hubble Space Telescope when it was first deployed in 1990. The primary mirror was ground incorrectly by just 2.2 micrometers—literally a fraction of a wavelength of red light. Perkin-Elmer, the contractor, had a flawed null corrector device during the manufacturing process. They had to send up a space shuttle mission to install corrective optics, the COSTAR system, which essentially acted like a highly complex pair of glasses for the telescope. The precision required for the orbital rendezvous maneuvers on that servicing mission is just staggering. You have to calculate the Hohmann transfer orbits using Kepler's laws of planetary motion, and the delta-v requirements have to be perfectly optimized to conserve propellant. The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation dictates the exact mass ratio needed, which is an exponential function of the required velocity change divided by the exhaust velocity... \n\nBut, um... anyway. Yeah. It's the simplest two-dimensional manifold. The intrinsic geometry of a flat space means that the sum of the angles in any triangle will always be exactly 180 degrees, and parallel lines will never intersect. But when you move into non-Euclidean geometries, everything changes. On a sphere, which has positive curvature, the angles of a triangle add up to more than 180 degrees. And on a hyperbolic paraboloid—a saddle shape with negative curvature—they add up to less. \n\nThe topology of the universe itself is still a matter of debate among cosmologists. Is it flat, open, or closed? The cosmic microwave background radiation data from the Planck satellite suggests that the observable universe is incredibly close to being spatially flat, with a margin of error of just about 0.4 percent. This flatness problem was actually one of the main catalysts for the theory of cosmic inflation. If the early universe underwent an exponential expansion in a fraction of a second, it would have stretched out any initial curvature, making the universe appear flat to us today, much like how the Earth appears flat from our localized perspective on the surface. The scalar field driving that inflation, the inflaton field, would have to have very specific potential energy properties to roll down the energy curve at just the right rate...\n\nBut, uh, yes. You're dealing with coupled non-linear partial differential equations to simulate fluid dynamics in the atmosphere and oceans. The Navier-Stokes equations, for instance, are notoriously difficult to solve. They describe the motion of viscous fluid substances, and the existence and smoothness of solutions to these equations in three dimensions is actually one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems in mathematics. If you can prove it, the Clay Mathematics Institute will give you a million dollars. \n\nThe turbulence modeling is the real bottleneck. Lorenz was a meteorologist, you know, and he discovered strange attractors while running weather simulations on a Royal McBee LGP-30 computer in the 1960s. The Lorenz attractor looks like a butterfly, ironically enough. It's a fractal structure, meaning it has a non-integer dimension. Fractals are everywhere in nature—coastlines, snowflakes, the branching of blood vessels... \n\nBut, um, yes. The contract. The speed of sound in dry air at standard atmospheric pressure is roughly 343 meters per second, but that changes depending on the temperature and the density of the medium. In water, it's over four times faster. \n\nThat's the fundamental principle behind sonar, actually—Sound Navigation and Ranging. Submarines use it to navigate and detect targets in the deep ocean. They send out an acoustic pulse, a 'ping', and measure the time it takes for the echo to return. If the target is moving, the frequency of the return echo will be altered due to the Doppler effect. Christian Doppler described that mathematically in 1842. It's the same reason an ambulance siren noticeably drops in pitch as it drives past you on the street. The sound waves get compressed as the vehicle approaches and stretched out as it recedes. The precision required for the orbital rendezvous maneuvers on that servicing mission is just staggering. You have to calculate the Hohmann transfer orbits using Kepler's laws of planetary motion, and the delta-v requirements have to be perfectly optimized to conserve propellant. The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation dictates the exact mass ratio needed, which is an exponential function of the required velocity change divided by the exhaust velocity... \n\nBut, um... anyway. Yeah. It's the simplest two-dimensional manifold. The intrinsic geometry of a flat space means that the sum of the angles in any triangle will always be exactly 180 degrees, and parallel lines will never intersect. But when you move into non-Euclidean geometries, everything changes. On a sphere, which has positive curvature, the angles of a triangle add up to more than 180 degrees. And on a hyperbolic paraboloid—a saddle shape with negative curvature—they add up to less. \n\nThe topology of the universe itself is still a matter of debate among cosmologists. Is it flat, open, or closed? The cosmic microwave background radiation data from the Planck satellite suggests that the observable universe is incredibly close to being spatially flat, with a margin of error of just about 0.4 percent. This flatness problem was actually one of the main catalysts for the theory of cosmic inflation. If the early universe underwent an exponential expansion in a fraction of a second, it would have stretched out any initial curvature, making the universe appear flat to us today, much like how the Earth appears flat from our localized perspective on the surface. The scalar field driving that inflation, the inflaton field, would have to have very specific potential energy properties to roll down the energy curve at just the right rate...\n\nBut, uh, yes. You're dealing with coupled non-linear partial differential equations to simulate fluid dynamics in the atmosphere and oceans. The Navier-Stokes equations, for instance, are notoriously difficult to solve. They describe the motion of viscous fluid substances, and the existence and smoothness of solutions to these equations in three dimensions is actually one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems in mathematics. If you can prove it, the Clay Mathematics Institute will give you a million dollars. \n\nThe turbulence modeling is the real bottleneck. Lorenz was a meteorologist, you know, and he discovered strange attractors while running weather simulations on a Royal McBee LGP-30 computer in the 1960s. The Lorenz attractor looks like a butterfly, ironically enough. It's a fractal structure, meaning it has a non-integer dimension. Fractals are everywhere in nature—coastlines, snowflakes, the branching of blood vessels... \n\nBut, um, yes. The contract. It's purely mechanical—longitudinal waves of pressure propagating through a medium like air or water. Unlike electromagnetic radiation, which can travel through the vacuum of space, sound absolutely requires matter to vibrate. The speed of sound in dry air at standard atmospheric pressure is roughly 343 meters per second, but that changes depending on the temperature and the density of the medium. In water, it's over four times faster. \n\nThat's the fundamental principle behind sonar, actually—Sound Navigation and Ranging. Submarines use it to navigate and detect targets in the deep ocean. They send out an acoustic pulse, a 'ping', and measure the time it takes for the echo to return. If the target is moving, the frequency of the return echo will be altered due to the Doppler effect. They line the walls, floor, and ceiling with these deep, wedge-shaped fiberglass acoustic absorbers. The geometry of the wedges is critical because it forces the sound waves to bounce back and forth deep within the structure of the foam, dissipating the acoustic energy as trace amounts of heat. Microsoft actually built the quietest place on Earth at their headquarters in Washington. The background noise level there is negative 20.6 decibels. It's so quiet that you can hear your own heartbeat, the blood rushing through your veins, and even the grinding of your bones when you move. It's fascinating, but people who go in there often start experiencing sensory deprivation hallucinations within just a few minutes. The brain is essentially a pattern-recognition engine, and when you deprive it of external stimuli, it just starts generating its own internal signals to compensate. It's the same mechanism behind phantom limb pain in amputees. The rate of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion—the ADME profile—is all governed by differential equations. It's really just a specialized application of mass transfer kinetics. The liver, for instance, acts as this incredible biochemical reactor. The cytochrome P450 enzymes in the hepatic cells are responsible for metabolizing the vast majority of xenobiotics. They catalyze the oxidation of organic substances. The molecular docking simulations they run now to predict how a new drug molecule will bind to those enzyme active sites require immense computational power. They use Monte Carlo algorithms to sample all the possible conformational states of the protein-ligand complex. It's basically a highly sophisticated optimization problem, trying to find the lowest free energy state of the system. \n\nIt reminds me of the protein folding problem, actually. For decades, it was considered computationally intractable to predict a protein's three-dimensional structure just from its amino acid sequence. The number of possible conformations is astronomically large—Levinthal's paradox, they call it. If a protein tried every possible fold sequentially, it would take longer than the age of the universe to find the right one. But in reality, they fold in milliseconds. Now, with deep learning models like AlphaFold, they've practically solved it using attention-based neural networks...\n\nBut, uh, no. I haven't started any new medications. It's a Schmidt-Cassegrain design. Beautiful piece of engineering, really. It uses a catadioptric optical system, which combines a primary spherical mirror with a secondary convex mirror and a refractive corrector plate to eliminate spherical aberration. Spherical aberration is a fascinating optical flaw. It happens when incoming parallel light rays striking the outer edges of a spherical mirror focus at a slightly different point along the optical axis than the rays striking the center. It completely ruins the image resolution, creating this soft, blurred halo effect. \n\nThat's exactly what happened with the Hubble Space Telescope when it was first deployed in 1990. The primary mirror was ground incorrectly by just 2.2 micrometers—literally a fraction of a wavelength of red light. Perkin-Elmer, the contractor, had a flawed null corrector device during the manufacturing process. They had to send up a space shuttle mission to install corrective optics, the COSTAR system, which essentially acted like a highly complex pair of glasses for the telescope. The precision required for the orbital rendezvous maneuvers on that servicing mission is just staggering. You have to calculate the Hohmann transfer orbits using Kepler's laws of planetary motion, and the delta-v requirements have to be perfectly optimized to conserve propellant. The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation dictates the exact mass ratio needed, which is an exponential function of the required velocity change divided by the exhaust velocity... \n\nBut, um... anyway. Yeah. I just don't feel the pull to take the cover off it anymore. You're dealing with coupled non-linear partial differential equations to simulate fluid dynamics in the atmosphere and oceans. The Navier-Stokes equations, for instance, are notoriously difficult to solve. They describe the motion of viscous fluid substances, and the existence and smoothness of solutions to these equations in three dimensions is actually one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems in mathematics. If you can prove it, the Clay Mathematics Institute will give you a million dollars. \n\nThe turbulence modeling is the real bottleneck. We use Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations, but you have to introduce turbulence models like the k-epsilon model to close the equations. It's essentially trying to predict the unpredictable. The chaotic nature of the system means that even minuscule changes in the initial conditions—like the famous butterfly effect coined by Edward Lorenz—can lead to vastly different outcomes over time. Lorenz was a meteorologist, you know, and he discovered strange attractors while running weather simulations on a Royal McBee LGP-30 computer in the 1960s. The Lorenz attractor looks like a butterfly, ironically enough. It's a fractal structure, meaning it has a non-integer dimension. Fractals are everywhere in nature—coastlines, snowflakes, the branching of blood vessels... \n\nBut, um, yes. The contract. That was about two years and two months ago, and that's when this all started.\n\nTask:\n- CONFIRMED: symptoms clearly present or strongly implied by the patient's words.\n- DENIED: symptoms the patient explicitly says they do NOT have\n  (e.g. \"No\", \"I don't\", \"I haven't\", \"never\").\n- Do NOT speculate. Just the normal ambient sounds, you know. \n\nSound is an interesting phenomenon, though, when you really break it down. It's purely mechanical—longitudinal waves of pressure propagating through a medium like air or water. Unlike electromagnetic radiation, which can travel through the vacuum of space, sound absolutely requires matter to vibrate. The speed of sound in dry air at standard atmospheric pressure is roughly 343 meters per second, but that changes depending on the temperature and the density of the medium. In water, it's over four times faster. \n\nThat's the fundamental principle behind sonar, actually—Sound Navigation and Ranging. Submarines use it to navigate and detect targets in the deep ocean. They send out an acoustic pulse, a 'ping', and measure the time it takes for the echo to return. If the target is moving, the frequency of the return echo will be altered due to the Doppler effect. Christian Doppler described that mathematically in 1842. It's the same reason an ambulance siren noticeably drops in pitch as it drives past you on the street. The sound waves get compressed as the vehicle approaches and stretched out as it recedes. We actually use the exact same principle in astrophysics, but with light waves instead of sound, to measure the redshift of distant galaxies. Edwin Hubble used the relativistic Doppler effect to prove the universe is expanding, which completely upended Einstein's cosmological constant... \n\nBut, ah, to answer your question, no. I don't hear anyone speaking when there's nobody around. Just my own thoughts.\n\nTask:\n- CONFIRMED: symptoms clearly present or strongly implied by the patient's words.\n- DENIED: symptoms the patient explicitly says they do NOT have\n  (e.g. \"No\", \"I don't\", \"I haven't\", \"never\").\n- Do NOT speculate.
